query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of Ti to the equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy can induce an 'inverted' microstructure consisting of a continuous BCC matrix with discrete B2 precipitates, thereby improving room-temperature ductility without compromising high‐temperature strength or irradiation resistance by enhancing grain boundary cohesion and deflecting crack propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent high-temperature (≈1600°C) mechanical properties but very poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low-level Ti addition followed by an optimized heat-treatment to promote the formation of discrete B2 precipitates within the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Evaluations performed at room temperature (for ductility), at 1600°C (for yield strength and high-temperature stability), and under irradiation exposure (simulated ion irradiation conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: The Ti addition promotes a microstructural transition from a continuous ordered phase to a dual-phase microstructure where discrete B2 precipitates are dispersed in a continuous BCC matrix, enhancing grain boundary cohesion.
generation.mechanism: Ti modifies interfacial chemistry and local lattice stresses, leading to improved grain boundary cohesion and deflection of crack propagation; this microstructural change enhances dislocation mobility and delays crack initiation at room temperature while preserving the high melting point and phase stability at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the untreated NbMoTaW baseline (with room-temperature plastic strains around 2–4%), the modified alloy is expected to exhibit significantly increased room-temperature ductility (potentially >10% strain) while maintaining high-temperature yield strength (around 400 MPa at 1600°C) and unchanged irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC alloy characterized by low room temperature ductility and excellent high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The positive effect is anticipated only for low-level Ti additions (approximately 5–10 at%). Exceeding this range could destabilize the BCC matrix or lead to excessive formation of secondary phases, which might degrade the high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimum Ti concentration and the necessary heat treatment parameters for achieving the desired microstructure require experimental calibration. Additionally, the long-term evolution of the microstructure under sustained irradiation is not fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set of the baseline equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy and another set with a 5–10 at% Ti addition. Process both sets under identical heat-treatment conditions designed to promote the microstructural transformation to an inverted BCC+B2 structure. Perform room-temperature tensile/compressive tests, high-temperature mechanical tests at 1600°C, and controlled ion irradiation experiments.
measurements: Room-temperature ductility (measured by tensile/compressive strain to failure)
Irradiation-induced hardening and defect evolution (e.g., via ion irradiation and subsequent hardness or microstructural analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to the baseline, or if there is a significant degradation in the high-temperature mechanical strength or irradiation resistance, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [].
